newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLOS WELL-SUPPORTED 'HOLD' IN CALM MARKET - TRADERS.
newsitem.headline: OLOS WELL-SUPPORTED 'HOLD' IN CALM MARKET - TRADERS.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures will continue to be sensitive to any shock comments from EU leaders and finance ministers meeting in Amsterdam, traders said at the end of a quiet, mildly firmer Monday.

But no upsets were expected, especially after the finance ministers reached a compromise deal on a job creation and growth chapter in an update to the Maastricht Treaty, while securing EU-wide endorsement for the post-euro stability pact.
The compromise is expected to get the backing from the EU leaders, keeping the 15-nation bloc on course for the start of an economic and monetary union by 1999 [EEC-EMU].

There was no notable market reaction to the news of the compromise. "It was in line with expectations...in this sort of market it is best to stay calm, if you become aggressive you are only going to lose money," a trader said.
Some volatility was still possible before the end of the meeting, scheduled for Tuesday, but the uptrend for OLOs was unlikely to be disturbed. "Just hold on," he said.
Traders were looking to make money arbitraging small spread moves, especially at the short end versus Bunds, but otherwise there was not much scope for a quick buck.
The trader expected a flattening trend seen in Bunds versus Bobls in recent days to cross into OLOs. "If the market continues to rise, it must come our way too. We will see further flattening too."

Before investors would take action, however, they would want to see more U.S. data [US-MCE] to determine whether further support might come from Treasuries. U.S. CPI and industrial output figures are due on Tuesday and are expected to confirm that U.S. interest rates will be on hold for now [US&FCAST].
Once the U.S. data were out of the way, the focus would swing back to European issues, an analyst said.

"Even if an agreement is reached (in Amsterdam), uncertainty will remain over Germany's ability to reduce its budget deficit below three percent of GDP...this would increase the chances of a weaker EMU as Germany will be unable to prevent other countries which do not meet the budget criterion from participating in the first wave," he said.

However, only a major disagreement over the future of EMU would spark an outspoken sell-off in the core bond markets belonging to the mark bloc, he added. The chances of that happening were slim, making OLOs a 'hold' for now.
The benchmark 10-year OLO yielded 5.75 percent at 1450 GMT, down a tick from Friday's 5.76 percent. Front month OLO futures firmed four basis points to 122.36.
"5.75 percent should be a selling point for OLOs," a trader said, noting the paper had risen near two full points from the end of May, justifying some profit-taking.
